description: Atomic claims: one proposition each. 'asserts' is what the claim says in slot terms; it becomes a constraint resting on the claim itself. A claim with 'truth_slot' may be false: whether it is true is a slot of its own. 'derived' claims are conclusions the player earns by proving them, not clues to collect. 'attested' says who told it, how, and in which scene the reader learns it.

claims.text: Straker rode in Ross's colours for five years as a jockey, until he grew too heavy.

source:
rode in Colonel Ross’s colours before he became too
      heavy for the weighing-chair

claims.text: Straker has trained for the Colonel at King's Pyland for seven years.

source: for seven as trainer

claims.text: Straker has always shown himself a zealous and honest servant.

source:
has always shown
      himself to be a zealous and honest servant
I have always found him an excellent servant.

claims.text: Straker is married, has no children, keeps one maid-servant, and lives in a small villa about two hundred yards from the stables.

source:
John Straker, who is a married man, lived in a small

claims.text: Straker is comfortably off.

source: keeps one maid-servant, and is comfortably off

source:
One of these lads sat up each night in the stable,

claims.text: Every precaution was taken at King's Pyland to guard the favourite.

source:
Every precaution was taken
      to guard the favourite

source:
Tavistock itself lies two

source:
built by a

claims.text: Mapleton belongs to Lord Backwater and is managed by Silas Brown.

source:
which

source:
has brought in turn each of the prizes of the turf to

source:
the

claims.text: Many people had the strongest interest in keeping Silver Blaze from the start next Tuesday.

source:
there were many people who had the strongest interest in

claims.text: King's Pyland has two horses in for the Wessex Cup: Silver Blaze and Bayard.

source:
You’ve two horses in for the Wessex Cup—Silver Blaze

claims.text: Desborough, the Mapleton horse, is second in the betting.

source: As Desborough, their horse, was second in the betting

source:
He was a man of excellent

declared that he had no

He did not attempt to deny that he had acted as

source:
He is not a stranger to the district. He has twice lodged

claims.text: Simpson says the folded paper was a ten-pound note; one was found in his purse.

source:
He says that it was a ten-pound note. One was found in his
      purse

claims.text: Simpson acknowledges the cravat is his.

source: He acknowledges that it is his

claims.text: Simpson declares that he had lost the cravat.

source:
declares that he had lost

source:
When confronted with his cravat, he turned very

source:

claims.text: Simpson's stick is a Penang-lawyer weighted with lead — just such a weapon as could have made the head wounds by repeated blows.

his stick, which

claims.text: There is no wound on Simpson.

source: there was no wound upon his person
He has neither a knife nor any sign of a wound

claims.text: Simpson has no knife.

source: He has neither a knife nor any sign of a wound

source: The key, having served its purpose, would be hurled away

claims.text: Gregory says the opium was probably brought from London.

source:
The opium was probably brought from
      London

claims.text: Nothing connects Simpson with the interests of the Mapleton stables.

source: Nothing at all.

claims.text: Silas Brown is known to have large bets on the race, and he was no friend to Straker.

source:
Silas Brown, the trainer, is known to have had large bets upon the event, and

claims.text: As Desborough was second in the betting, Mapleton had an interest in the favourite's disappearance.

source:
they had
      an interest in the disappearance of the favourite

claims.text: The police have examined the Mapleton stables and found nothing to connect Brown with the affair.

source:
We have, however, examined the

claims.text: Gregory has examined every stable and out-house in Tavistock and for ten miles round.

source:
examined every stable and out-house in Tavistock, and for a

claims.text: Traces show a party of gypsies camped on Monday night within a mile of the spot where Straker died.

source:
We have found traces which show that a party of gypsies encamped

source: On Tuesday they were gone

claims.text: The moor is being scoured for the gypsies.

source: The moor is being scoured for these gypsies

source:
although a large reward has been offered, and

claims.text: A large reward has been offered for the horse.

source: a large reward has been offered

claims.text: Hunter's supper was a dish of curried mutton.

source:
his supper, which consisted of a dish of curried
      mutton

source:
She took no liquid, as there was a water-tap in the
      stables, and it was the rule that the lad on duty should drink
      nothing else

claims.text: The people at the house ate the same dish that night with no ill effect.

source:
the people at the house partook of the same
      dish on the same night without any ill effect

claims.text: Analysis shows an appreciable quantity of powdered opium in the remains of Hunter's supper.

source:
an analysis has shown that the remains of his

      powdered opium

claims.text: The opium was in Hunter's portion: it is the remains of his supper that were drugged.

source:
the remains of his
      supper left by the stable-lad

claims.text: The horses were exercised and watered as usual, and the stables locked up at nine.

source: the stables were locked up at nine o’clock

claims.text: Two of the lads walked up to the trainer's house and had supper in the kitchen.

source:
Two of the
      lads walked up to the trainer’s house, where they had supper in
      the kitchen

claims.text: Ned Hunter remained on guard in the stable.

source: the third, Ned Hunter, remained on guard

claims.text: A few minutes after nine, Edith Baxter carried Hunter's supper down to the stables, with a lantern because it was very dark and the path crossed the open moor.

source:
At a
      few minutes after nine the maid, Edith Baxter, carried down to

claims.text: Within thirty yards of the stables a man came out of the darkness and called to her to stop.

source:
Edith Baxter was within thirty yards of the stables, when a man
      appeared out of the darkness and called to her to stop

claims.text: The stranger was of gentlemanly bearing, in a grey tweed suit, cloth cap and gaiters, carrying a heavy stick with a knob; very pale and nervous; rather over thirty than under.

source:
she saw that he was a person of gentlemanly bearing, dressed in a
      grey suit of tweeds, with a cloth cap

claims.text: The stranger knew that a stable-boy sleeps there alone every night, and guessed the supper was his.

source:
I understand
      that a stable-boy sleeps there alone every night

claims.text: He took a folded white paper from his waistcoat pocket and offered Edith the prettiest frock money could buy if the boy had it that night.

source:
He took a piece of white paper folded up out of his
      waistcoat pocket

claims.text: Frightened, Edith ran past him to the window where she always handed in the meals. It was already open, and Hunter sat at the small table inside.

source:
It was already opened, and Hunter was seated at the
      small table inside

claims.text: Edith swears that as the stranger spoke at the window she saw the corner of the little paper packet in his closed hand.

source:
The girl has sworn that as he spoke she
      noticed the corner of the little paper packet protruding from his
      closed hand

claims.text: At the window the stranger asked Hunter for the straight tip on Silver Blaze and Bayard — was it true that Bayard could give the other a hundred yards in five furlongs?

source:
Is it a fact that at the weights Bayard could give the

claims.text: 'You're one of those damned touts!' Hunter sprang up and rushed across the stable to unloose the dog.

source:
He sprang up and
      rushed across the stable to unloose the dog
So, you’re one of those damned touts!

claims.text: A dog is kept in the stable.

source: when Hunter rushed out with the hound

claims.text: As Edith fled she looked back and saw the stranger leaning through the window.

source:
The girl fled away
      to the house, but as she ran she looked back and saw that the
      stranger was leaning through the window

claims.text: A minute later, when Hunter rushed out with the hound, the stranger was gone; Hunter ran all round the buildings and found no trace of him.

source:
A minute later, however,
      when Hunter rushed out with the hound he was gone

claims.text: Hunter locked the stable door before he ran out with the dog.

source:
The
      boy locked the door before he left it

claims.text: The stable window is not large enough for a man to get through.

source:
The window, I may add, was
      not large enough for a man to get through

claims.text: Hunter waited until the other lads returned, then sent a message to the trainer about what had happened.

source:
Hunter waited until his fellow-grooms had returned, when he sent

claims.text: Straker was excited at the account and left vaguely uneasy, though he did not seem to realise its true significance.

source:
It left him, however,

Straker
      was excited at hearing the account

claims.text: Hunter is certain that the stranger drugged his curried mutton while standing at the window.

source:
He was equally certain that
      the same stranger had, while standing at the window, drugged his
      curried mutton

claims.text: Hunter ate from his supper: the remains he left were analysed.

source:
the remains of his
      supper left by the stable-lad

source:
Mrs. Straker, waking at one in the morning,
      found that he was dressing

claims.text: Straker told his wife he could not sleep for anxiety about the horses and would walk down to see all was well.

source:
he said
      that he could not sleep on account of his anxiety about the
      horses

claims.text: Mrs. Straker could hear the rain pattering against the window, and begged him to stay.

source:
she could
      hear the rain pattering against the window

claims.text: In spite of her entreaties he pulled on his large mackintosh and left the house.

source:
in spite of her
      entreaties he pulled on his large mackintosh and left the house

source:
His wife tells us that the knife had

claims.text: Mrs. Straker woke at seven to find her husband had not come back; she dressed, called the maid, and set off for the stables.

source:
Mrs. Straker awoke at seven in the morning, to find that her

claims.text: When Mrs. Straker reached the stables that morning, the door was open.

source: set off for the stables. The door was open

claims.text: Inside, Hunter was huddled on a chair in a state of absolute stupor.

source:
huddled together upon a chair, Hunter was sunk in a state of
      absolute stupor

claims.text: The favourite's stall was empty, and there was no sign of the trainer.

source:
the favourite’s stall was empty, and there were
      no signs of his trainer

claims.text: Silver Blaze's bridle is missing.

source: His bridle is missing

claims.text: The two lads asleep in the chaff-cutting loft heard nothing in the night; they are both sound sleepers.

source:
They had heard nothing during
      the night, for they are both sound sleepers

claims.text: At first they hoped the trainer had taken the horse out for early exercise.

source:
the trainer had for some reason taken out the
      horse for early exercise

claims.text: From the knoll they saw Straker's overcoat flapping from a furze-bush, about a quarter of a mile from the stables.

source:
John Straker’s
      overcoat was flapping from a furze-bush

claims.text: The coat was laid across the bush.

source: Yes, it was laid across the bush.

claims.text: Just beyond the bush, at the bottom of a bowl-shaped hollow, lay Straker's body.

source:
at the bottom of
      this was found the dead body of the unfortunate trainer

claims.text: Straker's head had been shattered by a savage blow from some heavy weapon.

source:
His head
      had been shattered by a savage blow from some heavy weapon

claims.text: Straker had a long, clean cut on the thigh, made by some very sharp instrument.

source: inflicted evidently by some very sharp instrument

claims.text: In his right hand Straker held a small knife clotted with blood up to the handle.

source:
in his right hand he held a small knife, which
      was clotted with blood up to the handle

source:
in his left he
      clasped a red and black silk cravat

claims.text: The maid recognised the cravat as the one the stranger wore the evening before.

source:
which was recognised by the

claims.text: Hunter, on recovering, was quite positive the cravat was the stranger's.

source:
Hunter, on recovering from his stupor, was also quite positive

claims.text: Abundant marks in the mud at the bottom of the hollow show the horse was there at the time of the struggle.

source:
there were abundant proofs in the mud

claims.text: Watson suggests the cut on Straker's thigh may have been made by his own knife, in the convulsions after a brain injury.

source:
Is it not possible,” I suggested, “that the incised wound upon

claims.text: The police have concluded that Straker wounded himself in his fall.

source:
We have quite come to the conclusion that he wounded himself in
      his fall.

claims.text: It seemed clear Straker had defended himself vigorously against his assailants.

source:
It was clear,

      assailants

claims.note: Reported as the papers' reading; the truth is that there was no struggle with a man.

claims.text: That Straker had defended himself vigorously is the police reading of the knife in his hand, not something seen.

source: Straker had defended himself vigorously

claims.text: That there was more than one assailant is part of the same reading; nothing seen says so.

source:
against his

claims.text: Gregory arrested Fitzroy Simpson at the villas.

source:
he promptly found and arrested the man upon whom suspicion

claims.text: On Tuesday evening Holmes received telegrams from both Colonel Ross and Inspector Gregory.

source:
On Tuesday evening I received telegrams from both Colonel Ross,
      the owner of the horse, and from Inspector Gregory

claims.text: Holmes stayed in London on Wednesday expecting the horse to be found, and its abductor to be Straker's murderer — a blunder, he says.

source:
From hour to hour yesterday I expected to
      hear that he had been found

claims.text: Straker's body was brought back to the house and lies upstairs.

source: Yes; he lies upstairs.

claims.text: The inquest is to be held tomorrow.

source: The inquest is to-morrow.

claims.text: Straker's pockets held a box of vestas, two inches of tallow candle, an A.D.P. briar pipe, a seal-skin pouch with half an ounce of long-cut Cavendish, a silver watch with a gold chain, five sovereigns, an aluminium pencil-case, a few papers, and an ivory-handled knife marked Weiss & Co., London.

source:
There was a box of
      vestas, two inches of tallow candle

claims.text: The bloodstained knife from Straker's hand is a cataract knife.

source: It is what we call a cataract knife

claims.text: It has a very delicate blade for very delicate work, and would not shut in a pocket.

source:
A strange thing for a man to carry with him upon a rough

claims.text: The knife's tip had been guarded by a disk of cork, found beside the body.

source:
The tip was guarded by a disk of cork which we found beside his

claims.text: Gregory thinks the knife was a poor weapon, but perhaps the best Straker could lay his hands on.

source:
It was a poor weapon, but perhaps the best that he
      could lay his hands on at the moment

claims.text: Straker's papers: three receipted hay-dealers' accounts, a letter of instructions from Colonel Ross, and a milliner's account.

source: Three of them are receipted hay-dealers’ accounts

claims.text: The milliner's account is for £37 15s, made out by Madame Lesurier of Bond Street to William Derbyshire.

source:
a milliner’s account for thirty-seven pounds fifteen made out by

claims.text: One item on the bill is a single costume at twenty-two guineas.

source:
Twenty-two guineas is rather

claims.text: Mrs. Straker says Derbyshire was a friend of her husband's, and his letters were sometimes addressed to the house.

source:
Mrs.

claims.note: Mrs. Straker believes it; it is false.

claims.text: Mrs. Straker says Derbyshire's letters were sometimes addressed to the house: what she saw herself.

source: occasionally his letters were addressed here

claims.text: Mrs. Straker says Derbyshire was a friend of her husband's: what she was told.

source: Derbyshire was a friend of her husband’s

claims.text: Holmes says he surely met Mrs. Straker at a garden-party in Plymouth some little time ago.

source:

claims.note: A deliberate test; Holmes explains it in s10.

claims.text: Mrs. Straker says she never had such a dress.

source: I never had such a dress, sir

claims.text: Mrs. Straker says Holmes is mistaken.

source: No, sir; you are mistaken.

claims.text: A woman waiting in the passage, haggard and eager, asks: 'Have you got them? Have you found them?'

source: Have you got them? Have you found them?

claims.text: There was no wind on Monday night, only very heavy rain.

source: None; but very heavy rain.

claims.text: A piece of matting was laid at the side of the hollow, and everyone has stood on it.

source:
A piece of matting has been laid here at the side, and we have

claims.text: In the trampled mud of the hollow lies a half-burned wax vesta, so coated with mud it looked like a chip of wood.

source:
It was a wax vesta half burned, which was so coated with
      mud that it looked at first like a little chip of wood

claims.text: Holmes found the vesta only because he was looking for it.

source:
I only saw it because I was
      looking for it

claims.text: Holmes compared Straker's boot and Simpson's shoe with the marks in the hollow.

source:
compared the impressions of

source:
I have examined the ground very carefully for a hundred yards in
      each direction

claims.text: This part of the moor is very hard and dry.

source:
This part of the moor, as the Inspector remarked,

claims.text: The ground falls away towards Mapleton into a long hollow that must have been very wet on Monday night.

source:
there is a long hollow over yonder, which
      must have been very wet on Monday night

source:
The track of a horse was
      plainly outlined in the soft earth in front of him, and the shoe
      which he took from his pocket exactly fitted the impression

claims.text: Beyond, the horse's tracks run on alone; near Mapleton a man's track appears beside them for the first time.

source: A man’s track was visible beside the horse’s.
The horse was alone before

claims.text: The double track, the horse's and the man's, turns sharp off and takes the direction of King's Pyland.

source:
The double track turned sharp off and took the direction of
      King’s Pyland

claims.text: The same tracks come back again in the opposite direction.

source:
the same tracks coming back
      again in the opposite direction

claims.text: The returning track ends at the paving of asphalt that leads up to the gates of the Mapleton stables.

source:
It ended at the paving of asphalt which led
      up to the gates of the Mapleton stables

claims.text: The man's prints have peculiarly square toes, and Silas Brown's own boots correspond exactly.

source:
you observed the peculiarly
      square toes in the impressions, and that his own boots exactly
      corresponded to them

claims.text: The groom says that if anyone at Mapleton is about at five in the morning it will be his master: he is always the first stirring.

source:
if any one is about he will be, for he is always
      the first stirring

claims.text: The groom dares not be seen taking Holmes's money: 'it is as much as my place is worth'.

source:
it is as much as my place is worth to

source: It’s a lie!” he shouted, “an infernal lie!

source:
Should I
      change it first or not?

claims.text: The lad who tends the paddock sheep says three of them have lately gone lame.

source:
not of much account; but three of them have gone

claims.text: The two lads in the loft heard nothing in the night, though a dog was kept in the stable.

source:
They had heard nothing during

claims.text: Nobody raised the alarm in the night: the lads in the loft heard nothing, and were roused only when Mrs. Straker came at seven.

source:
They had heard nothing during

The two lads who slept in the chaff-cutting loft above the
